title: Affirming Unattested Expertise at Ceiling Confidence: Auditing a Search-Augmented Answer Endpoint and Five Harness Failure Modes
description: Search-augmented answer APIs are increasingly queried to verify claims about named people, yet false affirmations carry asymmetric downstream costs in expert sourcing and due diligence. We audit one commercial answer endpoint (Exa /answer, one prompt and JSON schema, September 2026, 1250 calls) against verifiable authorship records in OpenAlex and employment filings under SEC Section 16. Asked whether a named researcher has published expertise in a topic, the endpoint confirms 0.9600 (95% Wilson [0.9279,0.9781]) of attested claims (n=250) while affirming claims with no matching work in the author's OpenAlex record at 0.1680 [0.1268,0.2193] for an adjacent subfield (NEAR), 0.1320 [0.0956,0.1796] for an adjacent field (FAR), and 0.0840 [0.0556,0.1250] for a different domain (CONTROL; n=250 each; post-hoc Cochran-Armitage trend z=2.81, p=0.0049 across unpaired draws). Schema-elicited confidence sits at ceiling (91.5% of main-run answers in [0.9, 1.0], mean 0.987 against accuracy 0.889) and performs worse than a constant base-rate forecast (Brier 0.1191 against 0.1005; post-hoc Brier Skill Score -0.1852). An unblinded single-reader inspection of all 21 different-domain affirmations finds 6 (0.0240) clearly attributable to endpoint error, with the rest reflecting broad topic labels or possible split author profiles; the measured rates are therefore upper bounds carrying unquantified error from OpenAlex's third-party classifier. Alongside the empirical findings, we document five measurement failure modes — wire-format mismatch, anchor leakage, parser artifacts, top-N negative contamination, and forced monotonicity — caught only by row-level and bin-level inspection. Every measurement describes one endpoint, one prompt, and one draw; code, results, and frozen pre-registrations are public. Not peer reviewed. Code and protocol: https://github.com/caiotheodoro/titer
